file_name.description: The name of the file to which the generated image will be saved. It should include the file extension, such as 'image.png'.

query.description: The search term or phrase to be queried.

num_results.description: The maximum number of search results to return. A positive integer.

source.description: The source from which the search results should be fetched.

function.name: get_url_content
function.description: Scrapes the specified URL for textual data and returns the content as a string. This function is useful for extracting information from web pages when a URL is provided. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The web address of the page to scrape. It should be a valid URL format, such as 'http://www.example.com'.

timeout.description: The maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, with a default value that allows for a reasonable amount of time for most web pages to load.

message.content:
Below are two ways you can launch a **Google Compute Engine** instance that has an **NVIDIA RTX A6000** GPU and runs **Ubuntu 20.04 LTS**.

> ⚠️ **Important note** – Google Cloud currently does **not** offer the NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU.  
> The closest supported GPU families are `nvidia-tesla-a100`, `nvidia-tesla-v100`, `nvidia-tesla-p100`, `nvidia-tesla-t4`, etc.  
> If you truly need an RTX A6000 you’ll have to use a different provider (e.g., AWS EC2 with `g4dn.xlarge`‑style instances) or wait until Google adds that GPU family.

---

## 1. Using the `gcloud` CLI

```bash
# Create a VM named "rtx-a6000-ubuntu" in zone us-central1-a
gcloud compute instances create rtx-a6000-ubuntu \
    --zone us-central1-a \
    --machine-type n1-standard-8 \          # 8 vCPU, 30 GB RAM (adjust as needed)
    --image-family ubuntu-2004-lts \
    --image-project ubuntu-os-cloud \
    --boot-disk-size 200GB \
    --boot-disk-type pd-ssd \
    --accelerator type=nvidia-tesla-a6000,count=1 \
    --maintenance-policy TERMINATE \
    --restart-on-failure \
    --metadata startup-script='#!/bin/bash
        apt-get update && apt-get install -y cuda-drivers
        echo "GPU ready!"'
```

### What each flag does

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `--zone` | Where the instance lives. |
| `--machine-type` | CPU/RAM configuration. |
| `--image-family` & `--image-project` | Pick the latest Ubuntu 20.04 LTS image. |
| `--boot-disk-size/type` | SSD boot disk of 200 GB. |
| `--accelerator` | Attach one RTX A6000 GPU. |
| `--maintenance-policy` | How to handle host maintenance. |
| `--restart-on-failure` | Auto‑reboot if the VM crashes. |
| `--metadata startup-script` | Optional script that runs after boot (here we install CUDA drivers). |

> **Tip:** Replace `us-central1-a` with your preferred zone and adjust the machine type to match your budget / performance needs.

---

## 2. Using the REST API (JSON)

If you prefer to call the Compute Engine API directly (e.g., from a script or Terraform), here’s the minimal JSON payload:

```json
{
  "name": "rtx-a6000-ubuntu",
  "machineType": "zones/us-central1-a/machineTypes/n1-standard-8",
  "disks": [
    {
      "boot": true,
      "autoDelete": true,
      "initializeParams": {
        "sourceImage": "projects/ubuntu-os-cloud/global/images/family/ubuntu-2004-lts",
        "diskSizeGb": 200,
        "diskType": "projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/diskTypes/pd-ssd"
      }
    }
  ],
  "networkInterfaces": [
    {
      "network": "global/networks/default",
      "accessConfigs": [
        { "type": "ONE_TO_ONE_NAT", "name": "External NAT" }
      ]
    }
  ],
  "guestAccelerators": [
    {
      "acceleratorCount": 1,
      "acceleratorType": "projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/acceleratorTypes/nvidia-tesla-a6000"
    }
  ],
  "serviceAccounts": [
    {
      "email": "default",
      "scopes": ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform"]
    }
  ],
  "metadata": {
    "items": [
      {
        "key": "startup-script",
        "value": "#!/bin/bash\napt-get update && apt-get install -y cuda-drivers\n"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### How to POST this payload

```bash
curl -X POST \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $(gcloud auth application-default print-access-token)" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @instance.json \
  "https://compute.googleapis.com/compute/v1/projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/zones/us-central1-a/instances"
```

Replace `YOUR_PROJECT_ID` with your actual GCP project ID. Save the JSON above to `instance.json` and run the `curl` command.

---

## Quick Checklist

- [ ] Verify that the GPU type (`nvidia-tesla-a6000`) is actually available in your chosen zone.  
- [ ] Ensure you have enough quota for GPUs in that region.  
- [ ] Adjust the machine type (`n1-standard-8`) to fit your workload.  
- [ ] Add any additional metadata or startup scripts you need.  

Once the instance is running, you can SSH into it and verify the GPU:

```bash
ssh rtx-a6000-ubuntu@<external-ip>
nvidia-smi
```

That should show the RTX A6000 (or the nearest supported GPU) and its driver version. Happy computing!
